title: Rotation Matrices Add Their Angles
topic: R(θ) parametrises rotations of the plane. Sweeping θ rotates the basis. Composing R(α) and R(β) gives R(α + β) — matrix multiplication becomes angle addition.

beats.narration: What does a rotation matrix actually do — and what happens when you multiply two of them?
The rotation matrix R of theta has cosine on the diagonal and sine off it, with one minus sign. Its columns are where e one and e two land after rotating by theta.

elements.content: Standard grid with e1 (violet) and e2 (teal) basis vectors at θ=0
R(θ) matrix shown in panel: [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]

beats.narration: Sweep theta from zero all the way around. The basis vectors trace circles. Both columns rotate together, locked ninety degrees apart — that is what keeps R orthogonal.

elements.content: θ sweeps from 0 to 2π. e1 traces a unit circle (violet trail). e2 traces the same circle, always 90° ahead (teal trail).
Live readout: θ = current angle. Matrix entries update to cos θ / sin θ.

beats.narration: Apply R of thirty degrees, then R of forty-five degrees. The grid rotates by seventy-five — the angles add. So the matrix product equals R of alpha plus beta. Matrix multiplication becomes angle addition.

elements.content: Unit square rotates by 30° first (intermediate), then by another 45° to reach 75°
R(30°) · R(45°) = R(75°) equation revealed once arrival angle is reached

beats.narration: A rotation matrix turns the plane by its angle. Multiplying two rotations adds their angles — geometry hiding inside matrix arithmetic.

elements.content: Matrix multiplication, written as angle addition.
